sections.html:
North central Utah holds Wasatch County, built around Heber Valley, a mountain-ringed basin on the Wasatch Back. Of its 1,206 square miles, 30 are water. Heber City is both seat and biggest city, and Midway and a piece of Park City also fall inside the line.

The county counted 34,788 people in 2020 and about 38,514 today, against 8,523 in 1980, and the 2020 figure ran 47.8% above 2010. Of 11,040 households in 2020, 76.3% were owner-occupied. Heber City sits at 5,601 feet and had 16,856 residents in 2020, and Midway had 6,003. About 27% of Heber City residents commute to Park City or Salt Lake City.

Some Midway subdivisions require a share of Swiss-style features on new houses. If you inherit or list a home there, ask about any subdivision design rules.

Responsibility is divided among three offices: the assessor puts a value on each parcel, the clerk/auditor sets rates and receives valuation appeals, and the treasurer collects payment. Value appeals are heard by the county council in its role as the Board of Equalization.

Property is assessed at 100% of fair market value as of January 1. Live in a home 183 or more consecutive days of the year and 45% of its value is exempt as a primary residence. Farmland that qualifies can be assessed on what it produces, with greenbelt applications due May 1.

Since the Truth in Taxation law of 1985, the system has been tied to revenue. A taxing entity that wants to collect more has to hold a public hearing first, and individual rates shift when county-wide values shift. The county's property tax system page has the official detail.

Mail a payment with a postmark of November 30 or earlier and there is no penalty. Online payments go through Instant Payments, and credit cards are not accepted.

  • Payments received December 1 through January 31 carry a 1% penalty.
  • Payments postmarked after January 31 carry a 2.5% penalty plus interest back to January 1.
  • Checks go to Wasatch County Treasurer, 25 N. Main, Heber City, UT 84032, with the parcel number written on them.

The office is open 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., Monday through Friday, at (435) 657-3218. Ask your mortgage company whether it is paying the tax, a detail that is easy to lose track of after a refinance or a loan sale.

A delinquent multiyear listing is posted by the treasurer and refreshed weekly. Since interest keeps running, payoff numbers move every day, so call (435) 657-3217 for the exact figure.

Applications reach the clerk/auditor by 5 p.m. on September 15, either through the website or at 25 North Main Street in Heber City. The statutory deadline is whichever comes later, September 15 or 45 days after notice, and the board then has 60 days to rule.

The county denies applications that arrive without evidence of your value estimate. Parcels with the same owner in the same general area can share one appeal, but each needs its own proof. Call the clerk/auditor at (435) 657-3190 with questions.

Not satisfied with the board's decision? A second appeal goes to the Utah State Tax Commission on Form TC-194, filed through the county auditor within 30 days. The statute is Utah Code 59-2-1004.

Long, snowy winters send a buyer's eyes straight to the roof, furnace and exposed pipes. About 75 inches of snow fall on Heber City in a year, spread over roughly 29 snowy days, with January at 21.5 inches and December at 17.8.

The average January high is 36.5 degrees and the low 12.5, and the record low is minus 38. July highs average near 89.5 degrees, and annual precipitation is about 15 inches.

Snow is no defect, but overdue roof, gutter or heating work on an older Heber Valley house is easy for an inspector to find. Owners who do not want to pay for it first often choose an as-is cash sale.

Before you sign a contract, get a payoff from the treasurer and compare it to the closing statement. The weekly delinquent listing shows quickly whether your parcel appears.

  • Find your latest tax notice and the July valuation notice.
  • Check with the mortgage servicer on whether escrow already covered this year's bill.
  • Phone (435) 657-3217 for a payoff figure on closing day.
  • Give the treasurer a current mailing address if the house is vacant or seasonal.

If back taxes, deferred repairs or the cost of carrying a second home are why you want out, we buy houses in Wasatch County as-is and can work around those problems.

sections.h2: How a closing handles the tax
sections.html:
At closing the title company takes the payoff out of your proceeds and sends it to the treasurer. Where you have already paid the year's bill, the settlement statement credits you for the months after closing. Where you have not, your share comes out of the sale. Bring the tax notice so the parcel number matches on every paper.

For a seasonal home, remember that notices go to the mailing address on file. A stale mailing address is how a small balance turns into a delinquent one.

sections.h2: What to gather before you list
sections.html: Start with three papers: the deed, the newest tax notice and the July valuation notice. Add anything that shows past repairs to the roof, furnace or plumbing. Write down your parcel number and keep it on the first page of the folder, since every county office will ask for it. If a mortgage company has been paying the tax, request its latest payment record so there are no surprises on the settlement statement.

sections.h2: Questions to ask before choosing a sale route
sections.html: Decide how soon you must close, what repairs a buyer would expect and whether the house could pass a lender's appraisal. Listing suits a well-kept house when time is on your side. Cash suits a house that needs work, a tax balance that is behind, or an owner too far away to manage showings through long snowy winters.

faqs.q: What is the Wasatch County property tax due date?
faqs.a: November 30. A payment postmarked by then has no penalty, and tax notices are mailed October 30. What you owe depends on your assessed value and the combined rate of the taxing entities serving your address.

faqs.q: Does Wasatch County give a break for a primary residence?
faqs.a: Yes, a 45% exemption applies to a home where you live 183 or more consecutive days in a year. The county wants exemption forms at the Assessor's Office before June.

faqs.q: When can I appeal my Wasatch County property value?
faqs.a: From August 1 through September 15, with a 5 p.m. cutoff on the last day. Include your own value estimate and supporting evidence, and file online or at 25 North Main Street in Heber City.

faqs.q: Can I pay Wasatch County property tax by credit card?
faqs.a: No. Pay online through Instant Payments, mail a check to 25 N. Main in Heber City, or visit the office on a weekday from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Wasatch County house if the taxes are unpaid?
faqs.a: Usually. The treasurer gives you a payoff amount at (435) 657-3217, and the title company pays it from your proceeds. A tax balance will not keep us from making an offer on a house here.
